Asynchronous On-Policy Self-Distillation

Xidong Wu Affiliation: University of Pittsburgh    Qi Qi Affiliation: University of Iowa    Yuqiong Ji Affiliation: University of Pennsylvania    Shangqian Gao Affiliation: Florida State University
Abstract

Unlike on-policy distillation (OPD), which depends on a separate teacher model, on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) leverages a single language model acting simultaneously as the student and the teacher, with the teacher conditioned on privileged information. Despite this architectural simplicity, synchronous rollout generation dominates overall training time, creating a severe systems bottleneck when scaling OPSD. To address this, we introduce Asynchronous On-Policy Self-Distillation (AsyncOPSD), a framework that decouples rollout generation from learner updates to improve training throughput. Since the teacher and student share parameters, AsyncOPSD eliminates the multi-model coordination overhead inherent to OPD architectures in asynchronous training. As the student policy evolves, buffered trajectories generated by older policies become stale, potentially degrading performance. To mitigate this, we introduce a distillation objective based on staleness-aware policy control and token-level entropy weighting. Across three model sizes and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, AsyncOPSD improves the training throughput by 1.961.96–2.25×2.25\times over synchronous OPSD while increasing average benchmark accuracy.

1 Introduction

On-policy distillation (OPD) has been used as an effective approach in the large language model (LLM) post-training Yang et al. (2025); Zeng et al. (2026); Gu et al. (2024). A student is trained on its own generated on-policy responses using token-level feedback from a teacher. Training on student-generated prefixes mitigates the train-test distribution shift inherent in distilling from fixed trajectories Agarwal et al. (2024). OPD typically uses a separate large teacher model while On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) instead instantiates both roles from a single language model. The privileged information, including a verified solution reasoning trace or feedback, augments the teacher’s context, while the student receives only the question. Matching their token-level distributions transfers the benefit of this additional context to the student without requiring an external teacher Zhao et al. (2026).

Despite this simplification, large-scale OPSD and OPD inherit the on-policy rollout bottleneck. Long reasoning traces dominate training time, and strict synchronization forces the learner to wait for new rollouts, leaving compute resources idle. While asynchronous execution improves utilization by generating rollouts and updating the learner concurrently, buffered trajectories quickly become stale. Training on this outdated data introduces a distribution mismatch and creates a performance–efficiency trade-off Kang et al. (2026). Recent work explores this trade-off in asynchronous OPD Wang et al. (2026); Rang et al. (2026); Kang et al. (2026). These studies highlight the importance of designing asynchronous pipelines. We study asynchronous execution for OPSD by overlapping rollout generation and learner-side privileged-context distillation under a fixed GPU budget.

We introduce Asynchronous On-Policy Self-Distillation (AsyncOPSD), a framework that decouples rollout generation from learner updates. Learners update model weights asynchronously from a shared replay buffer and periodically export the current policy (model weights), and distributed rollout actors generate trajectories after synchronizing the refreshed policy. At each update, learners evaluate buffered trajectories under both the student and a privileged teacher context. Computing teacher supervision on the learner side eliminates teacher-scoring stages and the communication overhead of transmitting cached teacher distributions, substantially simplifying system coordination compared to AsyncOPD Kang et al. (2026).

However, buffered sequences inevitably reflect the behavioral distribution of older policies. Our theoretical analysis bounds the discrepancy using prefix-distribution mismatch and an entropy-dependent loss bound. This motivates two complementary controls: 1) Staleness-Aware Policy Control: Limits the age of rollouts accepted for training; 2) Token-Level Entropy Weighting: Reduces the relative contribution of high-entropy teacher predictions. These techniques act on rollout selection and token-level loss weighting, respectively. Systematic ablation studies evaluate their efficacy. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    AsyncOPSD Framework: Introduced an asynchronous on-policy self-distillation architecture that overlaps rollout generation with optimization while computing privileged teacher supervision directly within the learner, removing the multi-model coordination overhead in asynchronous OPD training.

  • •

    Staleness & Uncertainty Mitigation: Analyzed how prefix staleness and teacher entropy enter an objective-discrepancy bound and proposed staleness-aware policy control and token-level entropy weighting to stabilize training.

  • •

    Empirical Acceleration: Evaluated AsyncOPSD across challenging reasoning benchmarks, achieving 1.961.96–2.25×2.25\times the sample throughput of synchronous OPSD and increasing average benchmark accuracy by 0.370.37–1.101.10 percentage points across three model sizes.

2 Related Work

2.1 On-Policy and Self-Distillation

On-policy distillation (OPD) reduces the mismatch between training and inference by supervising trajectories sampled from the student Agarwal et al. (2024); Gu et al. (2023); Lu and Lab (2025); Ko et al. (2024); Yang et al. (2026). Per-token KL-divergence feedback from a teacher model in the OPD also offers a dense learning signal at every step to reinforce sub-optimal reasoning. Recent studies optimize transfer efficiency via thinking-pattern compatibility Li et al. (2026c), teacher-entropy regularization Jin et al. (2026), and uncertainty-disagreement token filtering Xu et al. (2026). Other OPD efficiency methods adapt rollout horizons Tan et al. (2026) or combine rollout-depth control with turn-normalized supervision Zhou et al. (2026). Self-distillation extends self-taught reasoning paradigms Zelikman et al. (2022) by removing external teachers entirely, extracting supervision from self-generated reasoning traces Zhao et al. (2026), environment execution feedback Hübotter et al. (2026), hybrid reward-distillation objectives on failed rollouts Li et al. (2026a), or majority-vote pseudo-solutions Li et al. (2026d). POPO studies positive-only policy optimization with implicit negative gradients Xu and Fang (2026). Recent work examines reference-induced shortcuts Shen et al. (2026), reasoning degradation Kaur et al. (2026), reduced output diversity Nicolicioiu et al. (2026), and sensitivity to reasoning modes and teacher prefixes Li et al. (2026b) in OPSD. Broader OP(S)D diagnostics identify supervision mismatch and objective-dependent instability Zhu et al. (2026).

2.2 Asynchronous Reinforcement Learning

Decoupling rollout generation from policy optimization provides the foundation for scalable distributed RL Mnih et al. (2016); Espeholt et al. (2018). In LLM post-training, asynchronous architectures maximize accelerator utilization through pipeline overlapping Noukhovitch et al. (2025), worker load balancing Fu et al. (2026), disaggregated streaming generation Zhong et al. (2025), and dynamic trajectory repacking Sheng et al. (2026). To mitigate distribution mismatch caused by policy lag, algorithmic solutions employ proximal interpolation Li et al. (2025) and second-moment importance-weight bounding Zheng et al. (2026). However, while RL relies on scalar feedback, distillation depends on dense prefix-conditioned teacher distributions, creating distinct staleness dynamics.

2.3 Asynchronous On-Policy Distillation

Asynchronous OPD introduces coupled systems and distribution bottlenecks when integrating teacher evaluation into concurrent pipelines. Systems frameworks address these bottlenecks via pipelined scheduling Sheng et al. (2025) and distributed hidden-state streaming to reduce vocabulary communication Zhang et al. (2026). Algorithmically, AsyncOPD Kang et al. (2026) analyzes staleness under cached teacher scores, demonstrating divergence sensitivities and the inherent limits of action reweighting. Extending this, f-OPD Chen et al. (2026) separates policy drift from supervision drift using freshness weighting and adaptive refreshes and DivOPD Wang et al. (2026) prioritizes high-disagreement turns across stale queues.

However, asynchronous on-policy self-distillation is still underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce AsyncOPSD, which overlaps rollout generation and learner updates under a fixed GPU budget and simplifies distributed coordination by recomputing privileged teacher supervision directly within the learner.

3 Preliminaries

For next-token distributions pp and qq over vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V}, define DKL(p∥q)=∑v∈𝒱p(v)logp⁡(v)q⁡(v)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}p(v)\log\frac{p(v)}{q(v)}.

On-Policy Distillation.

On-policy distillation (OPD) Li et al. (2026c) trains a student pSp_{S} with parameters θ\theta using a separate, fixed teacher pTp_{T}. Given a prompt x∼𝒮xx\sim\mathcal{S}_{x}, where 𝒮x\mathcal{S}_{x} is the prompt dataset, the student samples y^∼pS(⋅∣x)\hat{y}\sim p_{S}(\cdot\mid x). Both models evaluate the same generated prefixes, yielding pS,n=pS(⋅∣x,y^<n)p_{S,n}=p_{S}(\cdot\mid x,\hat{y}_{<n}) and pT,n=pT(⋅∣x,y^<n)p_{T,n}=p_{T}(\cdot\mid x,\hat{y}_{<n}). The objective is

ℒOPD(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒮xy^∼pS(⋅∣x)[1|y^|∑n=1|y^|D(pT,n∥pS,n)]\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim\mathcal{S}_{x}\\ \hat{y}\sim p_{S}(\cdot\mid x)\end{subarray}}\!\left[\frac{1}{|\hat{y}|}\sum_{n=1}^{|\hat{y}|}D(p_{T,n}\|p_{S,n})\right]

commonly instantiated with reverse KL. The teacher remains fixed during training.

On-Policy Self-Distillation.

On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) Zhao et al. (2026) uses a single LLM as both teacher and student by conditioning on asymmetric prompt contexts: Student Policy pS(⋅∣x)p_{S}(\cdot\mid x): Observes only the original problem prompt xx, faithfully replicating inference conditions. Teacher Policy pT(⋅∣x,y⋆)p_{T}(\cdot\mid x,y^{\star}): Receives privileged context consisting of the question xx paired with verified reference reasoning, ground-truth answers y⋆y^{\star} or any other useful feedback.

Given problem-solution pairs (x,y⋆)(x,y^{\star}) from a reasoning dataset 𝒮\mathcal{S}, the student samples y^∼pS(⋅∣x)\hat{y}\sim p_{S}(\cdot\mid x). Using the divergence DD and setting pS,n=pS(⋅∣x,y^<n)p_{S,n}=p_{S}(\cdot\mid x,\hat{y}_{<n}) and pT,n=pT(⋅∣x,y⋆,y^<n)p_{T,n}=p_{T}(\cdot\mid x,y^{\star},\hat{y}_{<n}), the objective becomes

ℒOPSD(θ)=𝔼(x,y⋆)∼𝒮y^∼pS(⋅∣x)[1|y^|∑n=1|y^|D(pT,n∥pS,n)]\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPSD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}(x,y^{\star})\sim\mathcal{S}\\ \hat{y}\sim p_{S}(\cdot\mid x)\end{subarray}}\!\left[\frac{1}{|\hat{y}|}\sum_{n=1}^{|\hat{y}|}D(p_{T,n}\|p_{S,n})\right]

Gradients are backpropagated solely through the student policy pSp_{S}, while the privileged teacher pTp_{T} acts as a stop-gradient target.

4 AsyncOPSD: Framework, Analysis, and Method

4.1 Asynchronous Training Framework

Extending On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), we implement a baseline asynchronous variant (AsyncOPSD) by decoupling trajectory rollout generation from policy optimization across disjoint GPU pools. The GPU cluster is partitioned into the learner pool and the rollout actor pool. The learners execute forward passes, compute gradients, and optimize the model with the batch in the queue from rollout actors and periodically export the current policy (model weights). Concurrently, in the rollout actor pool, distributed rollout actors host independent, single-GPU vLLM instances to sample after loading the refreshed policy, pushing generated trajectories into a shared rollout queue.

Consistent with standard OPSD, no auxiliary teacher model is required; the student is optimized using a clipped forward-KL distillation objective. Model export frequency is governed by sync_step, enabling generation and gradient computation to overlap seamlessly at the cost of bounded policy staleness. To prevent memory overload and control queue delays, the system limits queue size based on learner microbatches.

4.2 Staleness–Entropy Analysis

Asynchronous training potentially degrades performance. We provide an analysis relating this degradation to student rollout staleness and the privileged teacher entropy. We first analyze the evolving shared-teacher formulation, in which privileged teacher and student predictions use the current parameters θk\theta_{k}. For the fair comparison in Section 5.1, we freeze the teacher policy to be the initial policy following the OPSD protocol Zhao et al. (2026). Appendix A.4 establishes the same form of staleness–entropy bound.

Shared-model formulation.

Let kk denote the learner update and r≤kr\leq k the policy version used for rollout generation. A training example consists of a problem xx and privileged information aa, such as a verified answer. For a response prefix y<hy_{<h},

sh\displaystyle s_{h} =(x,a,h,y<h),\displaystyle=(x,a,h,y_{<h}),
pk(⋅∣sh)\displaystyle p_{k}(\cdot\mid s_{h}) =πθk(⋅∣x,y<h),\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta_{k}}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<h}),
qk(⋅∣sh)\displaystyle q_{k}(\cdot\mid s_{h}) =πθk(⋅∣x,a,y<h).\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta_{k}}(\cdot\mid x,a,y_{<h}).

Teacher and student share the same model. The teacher output is detached during optimization. The per-prefix forward-KL loss is

Fk(s)=KL(sg[qk(⋅∣s)]∥pk(⋅∣s))F_{k}(s)=\operatorname{KL}\!\left(\operatorname{sg}[q_{k}(\cdot\mid s)]\,\middle\|\,p_{k}(\cdot\mid s)\right)

where sg\operatorname{sg} denotes stop-gradient. At a fixed kk, stop-gradient affects differentiation but not the numerical value of FkF_{k}. Let μr\mu_{r} and μk\mu_{k} be prefix distributions induced by the rollout and current policies, respectively. Both use the same distribution of (x,a)(x,a) and the same fixed distribution over token positions h∈{1,…,T}h\in\{1,\ldots,T\}. A finite horizon and a common continuation convention after termination make these distributions well-defined. We consider a fixed rollout version rr. The asynchronous and synchronous population objectives are

Jasynck\displaystyle J_{\mathrm{async}}^{k} =𝔼s∼μr​[Fk​(s)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mu_{r}}[F_{k}(s)], (1)
Jsynck\displaystyle J_{\mathrm{sync}}^{k} =𝔼s∼μk​[Fk​(s)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mu_{k}}[F_{k}(s)],
Δk\displaystyle\Delta_{k} =|Jasynck−Jsynck|.\displaystyle=\left|J_{\mathrm{async}}^{k}-J_{\mathrm{sync}}^{k}\right|.

This formulation follows the objective-discrepancy perspective of ff-OPD Chen et al. (2026), while specializing the supervision protocol. Both learner-side distributions are recomputed at θk\theta_{k} on the stored prefix.

The following theorem bounds the discrepancy between asynchronous and synchronous training objectives in terms of prefix staleness and teacher entropy, under the assumptions in Appendix A.

Theorem 1 (Joint staleness–entropy bound).

Fix a learner update kk and rollout version r≤kr\leq k, with the prefix laws and objectives in Eq. (1). Suppose Assumptions 1 and 2 hold, with B≥0B\geq 0 the uniform privileged logit contrast bound in Assumption 2. ρk,r​(sh)\displaystyle\rho_{k,r}(s_{h}) :=μk​(sh)μr​(sh)=∏u<hpk​(yu∣su)pr​(yu∣su),\displaystyle:=\frac{\mu_{k}(s_{h})}{\mu_{r}(s_{h})}=\prod_{u<h}\frac{p_{k}(y_{u}\mid s_{u})}{p_{r}(y_{u}\mid s_{u})}, (2)

The supporting assumptions, lemmas, and full proof are provided in Appendix A.

Discussion.

The bound motivates two complementary controls on prefix staleness and teacher entropy. The required signals are already available during training. We use the policy-version gap k−rk-r as an inexpensive proxy for prefix-distribution staleness, while teacher entropy is available from the existing teacher forward pass. Their joint use therefore requires no additional forward pass.

4.3 Staleness Control and Entropy Weighting

Staleness-Aware Policy Control.

Let kk be the current learner optimizer step and rir_{i} the step of the published policy that generated sample ii. Its staleness is si=max⁡{0,k−ri}s_{i}=\max\{0,k-r_{i}\}. We reject rollouts with a staleness sis_{i} greater than KK using the filter:

gK(τi)=𝟏{si≤K}g_{K}(\tau_{i})=\mathbf{1}\{s_{i}\leq K\}

where 𝟏​{⋅}\mathbf{1}\{\cdot\} is the indicator function. The learner rejects staleness above KK when claiming a queued rollout batch, fetching another batch until an admissible one is available. Generation and learning continue asynchronously. We set K=6K=6 based on the mean staleness in Table 1 and an ablation study in Section 5.6. Policy version gap is an inexpensive proxy for distribution drift.

Token-Level Entropy Weighting.

For an accepted completion token hh of rollout ii, write pi,hp_{i,h} for the current student distribution and qi,hq_{i,h} for the privileged fixed-teacher distribution. Both use temperature-scaled logits. Define teacher entropy:

Hi,h\displaystyle H_{i,h} =−∑v∈𝒱qi,h(v)logqi,h(v),\displaystyle=-\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}q_{i,h}(v)\log q_{i,h}(v),
ui,h\displaystyle u_{i,h} =exp(−βHHi,h),βH≥0.\displaystyle=\exp(-\beta_{H}H_{i,h}),\qquad\beta_{H}\geq 0.

Over all valid accepted completion positions 𝒜\mathcal{A} in each local learner microbatch, we normalize

wi,h=ui,h1|𝒜|​∑(j,m)∈𝒜uj,mw_{i,h}=\frac{u_{i,h}}{\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{(j,m)\in\mathcal{A}}u_{j,m}}

These weights reduce high-entropy tokens’ relative contribution and have mean one when the numerical floor is inactive. They reuse the teacher probabilities already computed for distillation. Setting βH=0\beta_{H}=0 recovers uniform weights. We retain per-token pointwise clipping in all conditions:

ℓc​(q,p)=∑v∈𝒱min⁡{q⁡(v)​log⁡q⁡(v)p⁡(v),c}\ell_{c}(q,p)=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\min\!\left\{q(v)\log\frac{q(v)}{p(v)},c\right\}

where c≥0c\geq 0 is the clipping threshold. Combining staleness filtering and token-level entropy weighting with this clipped loss gives the following objective, 𝒞\mathcal{C} is the set of candidate rollouts and TiT_{i} is the valid completion length of rollout ii. For rejected rollouts, set wi,h=0w_{i,h}=0 so that all terms below are defined:

ℒk=∑i∈𝒞gK​(τi)​∑h=1Tisg⁡[wi,h]​ℓc​(sg⁡[qi,h],pi,h)∑i∈𝒞gK​(τi)​Ti\mathcal{L}_{k}=\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}}g_{K}(\tau_{i})\sum_{h=1}^{T_{i}}\operatorname{sg}[w_{i,h}]\ell_{c}(\operatorname{sg}[q_{i,h}],p_{i,h})}{\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}}g_{K}(\tau_{i})T_{i}} (5)

where sg\operatorname{sg} denotes stop-gradient and normalization is over accepted tokens. The learner waits for accepted data if the denominator would be zero. The controls are motivated by the analysis, but do not constitute an exact correction of stale sampling. Entropy weighting changes the relative importance of tokens without changing the teacher target distribution, unlike the PMI target construction of Purified OPSD Shen et al. (2026). High-entropy positions can also support useful reasoning branches Kaur et al. (2026); downweighting them is a heuristic whose effect on reasoning diversity requires separate evaluation.

5 Experiments

We study the throughput–quality tradeoff of asynchronous on-policy self-distillation.

5.1 Experimental Setup

Models, data, and evaluation.

Following OPSD Zhao et al. (2026), we consider Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B, using the instruct-tuned versions. For training data, we use the mathematical reasoning subset of OpenThoughts Guha et al. (2026). We evaluate on AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and HMMT 2025 and report Avg@12. The details of the evaluation are shown in Table 5.

Implementation details.

As in Zhao et al. (2026), we use forward KL with full-vocabulary logit distillation with per-token pointwise KL clipping and the pointwise divergence clipping defined in Section 4.3. Following the OPSD protocol Zhao et al. (2026), we freeze the teacher at the initial model in all synchronous and asynchronous conditions to keep the teacher strategy matched across the empirical comparisons. The student receives the question in Thinking Mode (TM)-off, while the TM-on teacher additionally receives the reference solution.

All runs use eight NVIDIA A100 GPUs, rank-64 LoRA with bfloat16 precision, gradient checkpointing, and FlashAttention-2 for memory efficiency. Asynchronous execution allocates four GPUs to rollout actors and four to learners, with an effective global batch of 32. Synchronous OPSD uses all eight GPUs for alternating generation and optimization with the same effective global batch of 32. The training configuration is listed in Table 4. We repeat runs 3 times to get the mean and standard deviation to measure the throughput (samples/s) and the staleness.

Efficiency metrics.

We report accepted-training-sample throughput, Rsample=NacceptedTtrainR_{\mathrm{sample}}=\frac{N_{\mathrm{accepted}}}{T_{\mathrm{train}}}, where accepted samples are sequence occurrences actually consumed for optimization, and TtrainT_{\mathrm{train}} is the Trainer-measured training interval. Mean staleness uses sis_{i} from accepted rollout samples. Relative throughput is normalized to the recorded synchronous run for the same model, following the reporting style of asynchronous distillation studies Chen et al. (2026); Kang et al. (2026). We use sequences rather than response tokens, so our values are not numerically comparable to token-throughput results in AsyncOPD.

5.2 Policy Export Frequency

The sync_step specifies the learner policy export frequency and indirectly changes the mean staleness on the learner side. We compare sync_step∈{1,2,4,8}\texttt{sync\_step}\in\{1,2,4,8\} at a fixed 4/4 learner/actor allocation and effective batch 32, with policy control and entropy weighting disabled.

Table 1 shows the trade-off between throughput and staleness. Mean accepted-rollout staleness increases monotonically with sync_step for each model, whereas throughput does not. Changing sync_step from two to four increases mean throughput by only 2.0% and 1.6% for 1.7B and 4B and reduces it by 1.1% for 8B; mean staleness increases by 13.6%, 17.0%, and 17.5%, respectively. To get a high throughput without excessively sacrificing staleness, we select sync_step=2\texttt{sync\_step}=2 as a common throughput–freshness compromise in all experiments later.

5.3 Vanilla Asynchronous OPSD

Vanilla AsyncOPSD decouples generation from optimization. Actors generate with refreshed student policies and place rollouts in a shared queue; learners consume them, perform model training, and periodically export the policy. Only student LoRA adapters are published, avoiding full-model reloads on actors.

Table 2 reports the complete accuracy comparison, including the controlled variants discussed next. Vanilla asynchronous execution reduces the cross-benchmark average from 43.43 to 42.97 on 1.7B, from 63.60 to 62.30 on 4B, and from 64.80 to 64.23 on 8B. The decline is largest on 4B; it is not uniform across individual benchmarks. These results motivate controlling the optimization mismatch introduced by stale rollouts. The analysis in 4.2 provides a complementary motivation by identifying how prefix-distribution drift and teacher entropy interact in the objective discrepancy.

5.4 AsyncOPSD Ablation

We evaluate the strategies defined in Section 4.3. We disable the staleness limit and entropy weighting in vanilla AsyncOPSD. The Staleness Control baseline uses K=6K=6; Section 5.6 examines its throughput–freshness tradeoff. Full AsyncOPSD uses K=6K=6 and βH=0.1\beta_{H}=0.1. Setting βH=0\beta_{H}=0 disables entropy weighting. The clipping threshold is c=0.05c=0.05 for 1.7B/4B and c=0.06c=0.06 for 8B.

Results comparison.

Table 2 compares OPSD with the asynchronous variants. We select sync_step=2 to balance throughput and staleness. Staleness control alone raises the average over vanilla AsyncOPSD by 0.10, 1.13, and 0.67 percentage points on 1.7B, 4B, and 8B. Adding entropy weighting yields further gains of 0.73, 1.27, and 0.77 percentage points. AsyncOPSD reaches averages of 43.80, 64.70, and 65.67, exceeding OPSD by 0.37, 1.10, and 0.87 percentage points, respectively. Improvements are aggregate: for example, 1.7B HMMT25 slightly favors staleness control alone. This ablation measures the incremental benefit of entropy weighting with staleness control fixed at K=6K=6.

5.5 Training Throughput

Synchronous baseline.

To get a stronger baseline, we decouple synchronous generation batch size from training microbatch size to avoid unnecessarily restricting inference throughput. All three synchronous models generate 4 prompts per GPU per vLLM call. For 1.7B and 4B, the training microbatch is also 4, with one gradient-accumulation step. For 8B, we retain a training microbatch of 2 and 2 gradient-accumulation steps, while generating both microbatches together. This reduces the number of generation calls per GPU per optimizer update for 8B model from two to one without increasing the forward/backward microbatch. The generated responses are consumed within the same optimizer update, preserving synchronous execution and an effective global batch of 32.

Throughput and quality tradeoff.

Table 3 compares the updated synchronous baseline with all three asynchronous conditions. Synchronous OPSD achieves 4.07±0.324.07\pm 0.32, 2.40±0.332.40\pm 0.33, and 1.70±0.321.70\pm 0.32 samples/s on 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, respectively. Vanilla AsyncOPSD achieves 9.22, 5.53, and 3.61 samples/s, while AsyncOPSD achieves 8.00, 5.39, and 3.40 samples/s. Relative to the updated synchronous means, vanilla execution improves throughput by factors of 2.26, 2.31, and 2.12; staleness control alone achieves 2.01, 2.28, and 2.01 times the synchronous throughput. AsyncOPSD achieves 1.96×\times, 2.25×\times, and 1.99×\times throughput with reported average accuracy gains over OPSD of 0.37, 1.10, and 0.87 percentage points on 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, respectively. It retains 86.8%, 97.5%, and 94.2% of vanilla throughput. Relative to staleness control alone, entropy weighting changes mean throughput by −2.4-2.4%, −1.3-1.3%, and −0.9-0.9%.

Sources of throughput improvement.

The asynchronous implementation combines several systems changes. 1) Larger generation batches: Each rollout actor generates 32 completions per vLLM call, compared with four completions per GPU in the synchronous baseline. Larger batches can improve inference efficiency through higher GPU utilization. 2) Lower policy-refresh overhead. The synchronous implementation refreshes vLLM by merging the LoRA adapters every step. The asynchronous implementation instead exports only the updated LoRA adapters at a configurable sync_step. 3) Nonlinear learner scaling. Doubling the number of learner GPUs does not necessarily halve optimization time. Communication, synchronization, and small per-device workloads can limit scaling efficiency. Consequently, splitting GPUs into a learner pool and rollout actors pool can improve overall utilization despite using fewer GPUs for optimization. 4) Overlapping generation and optimization. Rollout actors generate upcoming batches while learners optimize previously generated samples. This overlap reduces idle periods associated with alternating generation and optimization in synchronous execution.

5.6 Ablation Study

GPU-Allocation Ablation.

Figure 2 shows the learner/actor allocation over 2/6, 3/5, 4/4, 5/3, and 6/2 on eight A100s with vanilla asynchronous execution. The balanced 4/4 allocation provides the highest mean sample throughput for each model: 8.63, 5.02, and 3.35 samples/s for 1.7B, 4B, and 8B. Allocating more GPUs to either generation or learning alone is insufficient: the two stages must supply and consume samples at compatible rates. We adopt 4/4 as a common operating point.

Staleness-Cutoff Ablation.

We sweep K∈{4,6,8,10}K\in\{4,6,8,10\} on Qwen3-1.7B with βH=0\beta_{H}=0. Throughput relative to the sweep’s K=6K=6 mean is 0.755, 1.000, 1.114, and 1.108, respectively. Increasing KK from 4 to 6 improves throughput by 32.4% and reduces rejection among claimed rollouts from 33.9% to 10.7%. Compared with K=8K=8, K=6K=6 retains 89.8% of throughput while reducing mean accepted-rollout staleness from 6.12 to 5.35; K=10K=10 provides no further mean throughput gain. For the tested values K = 8 and K = 10, no rejections occurred. It is similar to the vanilla AsyncOPSD. So we choose K=6K=6 as a conservative throughput–freshness compromise. Appendix B.1 reports the details.

Entropy-Weighting Ablation.

On Qwen3-1.7B, we select βH=0.1\beta_{H}=0.1 based on evaluation results among the tested coefficients {0.03,0.1,0.3,1.0}\{0.03,0.1,0.3,1.0\}. Full results are provided in Appendix B.2.

Conclusion

We introduced AsyncOPSD, which improves training efficiency by decoupling rollout generation from learner updates. Our analysis bounds the resulting objective discrepancy in terms of prefix staleness and teacher entropy, motivating staleness control and token-level entropy weighting. Across three model sizes and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, AsyncOPSD achieves 1.961.96–2.25×2.25\times the sample throughput of an optimized synchronous baseline while increasing average benchmark accuracy over OPSD by 0.370.37–1.101.10 percentage points.

Limitations

Our experiments use eight NVIDIA A100 GPUs and models ranging from 1.7B to 8B parameters. Within this budget, comparisons across three model sizes and targeted ablations provide evidence for the throughput benefits of asynchronous execution and the effectiveness of staleness control and entropy weighting in the evaluated settings. A broader exploration of model scales and training configurations is left to future work.

Appendix A Theoretical Analysis

This appendix supplies the sampling assumptions and intermediate lemmas used in Theorem 1, followed by its full proof. The learner update kk and rollout version r≤kr\leq k are fixed. The first three subsections evaluate both the student and privileged teacher at the current parameters θk\theta_{k} when computing the loss. Appendix A.4 extends the result to a teacher frozen at initialization, as used in our experiments.

A.1 Assumptions and prefix distributions

Assumption 1 (Common sampling protocol and coverage).

The rollout and current prefix laws use the same problem–reference distribution ν⁡(x,a)\nu(x,a), the same fixed token-position probabilities αh\alpha_{h} for h∈{1,…,T}h\in\{1,\ldots,T\}, and the same continuation convention after termination. Prefixes are generated autoregressively using the corresponding student policies prp_{r} and pkp_{k}, and μk≪μr\mu_{k}\ll\mu_{r}.

The notation μk≪μr\mu_{k}\ll\mu_{r} means absolute continuity. In the discrete prefix setting, it is the support condition

μr​(s)=0⟹μk​(s)=0.\mu_{r}(s)=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mu_{k}(s)=0.

Equivalently, every prefix with positive current-policy probability must also have positive rollout-policy probability. This condition allows the current prefix law to be represented by reweighting the rollout law; it does not compare the magnitudes of the probabilities. It concerns prefixes the rollout policy could generate, rather than requiring every such prefix to appear in a finite realized buffer.

Under Assumption 1, for j∈{r,k}j\in\{r,k\},

μj​(sh)=ν⁡(x,a)​αh​∏u<hpj​(yu∣su).\mu_{j}(s_{h})=\nu(x,a)\,\alpha_{h}\prod_{u<h}p_{j}(y_{u}\mid s_{u}). (6)

Full-support softmax sampling on a common vocabulary is sufficient for the coverage condition. The common problem and token-position factors cancel when comparing the two prefix laws.

Let zkS​(s)z_{k}^{S}(s) and zkT​(s)z_{k}^{T}(s) be the student and privileged teacher logits, respectively. They satisfy

pk\displaystyle p_{k} =softmax⁡(zkS),\displaystyle=\operatorname{softmax}(z_{k}^{S}), (7)
qk\displaystyle q_{k} =softmax⁡(zkT),\displaystyle=\operatorname{softmax}(z_{k}^{T}),
bk​(s)\displaystyle b_{k}(s) =zkT​(s)−zkS​(s).\displaystyle=z_{k}^{T}(s)-z_{k}^{S}(s).
Assumption 2 (Bounded privileged logit contrast).

There exists a finite constant B≥0B\geq 0 such that, at the analyzed update and uniformly over the support of μr\mu_{r},

osc⁡(bk​(s)):=maxv⁡bk,v​(s)−minv⁡bk,v​(s)≤B.\operatorname{osc}(b_{k}(s)):=\max_{v}b_{k,v}(s)-\min_{v}b_{k,v}(s)\leq B. (8)

The finite-support probability lower bound in Assumption 3.1 of ff-OPD Chen et al. (2026) is sufficient for this contrast condition when it holds on the same support used to evaluate the loss. Indeed, if pk​(v∣s),qk​(v∣s)≥ϵ>0p_{k}(v\mid s),q_{k}(v\mid s)\geq\epsilon>0, then

−log⁡(1/ϵ)≤log⁡qk​(v∣s)pk​(v∣s)≤log⁡(1/ϵ).-\log(1/\epsilon)\leq\log\frac{q_{k}(v\mid s)}{p_{k}(v\mid s)}\leq\log(1/\epsilon).

The vector bk​(s)b_{k}(s) differs from log⁡(qk/pk)\log(q_{k}/p_{k}) only by a common scalar, so its oscillation is at most 2​log⁡(1/ϵ)2\log(1/\epsilon). A lower bound imposed only on truncated distributions does not automatically imply the full-vocabulary condition. We state the contrast assumption directly because parameter sharing alone does not guarantee a small BB, and CB=B⁡(eB−1)/2C_{B}=B(e^{B}-1)/2 can be large when the admissible contrast is large.

A.2 Supporting lemmas

Lemma 1 (Change of measure and student staleness).

Under Assumption 1, define

ρk,r​(s)=μk​(s)μr​(s),dk,r​(s)=|1−ρk,r​(s)|.\rho_{k,r}(s)=\frac{\mu_{k}(s)}{\mu_{r}(s)},\qquad d_{k,r}(s)=|1-\rho_{k,r}(s)|. (9)

The prefix likelihood ratio satisfies

ρk,r​(sh)=∏u<hpk​(yu∣su)pr​(yu∣su).\rho_{k,r}(s_{h})=\prod_{u<h}\frac{p_{k}(y_{u}\mid s_{u})}{p_{r}(y_{u}\mid s_{u})}. (10)

Whenever the two objectives are finite,

Δk\displaystyle\Delta_{k} =|𝔼μr​[(1−ρk,r​(s))​Fk​(s)]|\displaystyle=\left|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}\left[(1-\rho_{k,r}(s))F_{k}(s)\right]\right| (11)
≤𝔼μr​[dk,r​(s)​Fk​(s)].\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}\left[d_{k,r}(s)F_{k}(s)\right].

Moreover, 𝔼μr​[dk,r​(s)]≤2\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}[d_{k,r}(s)]\leq 2.

Proof.

Dividing the factorizations in Eq. (6) cancels ν⁡(x,a)\nu(x,a) and αh\alpha_{h}, which gives Eq. (10). Absolute continuity ensures that the likelihood ratio exists μr\mu_{r}-almost everywhere and permits the change of measure

Jsynck=𝔼μr​[ρk,r​(s)​Fk​(s)].J_{\mathrm{sync}}^{k}=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}[\rho_{k,r}(s)F_{k}(s)].

Both objectives use exactly the same current loss Fk​(s)F_{k}(s); only the distribution over prefixes changes. Subtracting the last expression from JasynckJ_{\mathrm{async}}^{k} therefore yields the equality in Eq. (11). The triangle inequality and Fk​(s)≥0F_{k}(s)\geq 0 give its upper bound. Finally, since 𝔼μr​[ρk,r]=1\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}[\rho_{k,r}]=1,

𝔼μr​[dk,r]≤𝔼μr​[1+ρk,r]=2.\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}[d_{k,r}]\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}[1+\rho_{k,r}]=2.

Equivalently, this expectation is 2​TV⁡(μr,μk)2\operatorname{TV}(\mu_{r},\mu_{k}) under the convention TV⁡(P,Q)=12​‖P−Q‖1\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\tfrac{1}{2}\|P-Q\|_{1}. ∎

Lemma 2 (Entropy-sensitive self-distillation loss).

Under Assumption 2, the current forward-KL loss satisfies, for every prefix in the support of μr\mu_{r},

0≤Fk​(s)≤CB​(1−e−Hk​(s))≤CB​Hk​(s),0\leq F_{k}(s)\leq C_{B}(1-e^{-H_{k}(s)})\leq C_{B}H_{k}(s),

where Hk​(s)H_{k}(s) and CBC_{B} are defined in Eq. (2).

Proof.

Suppress k,sk,s and write p=softmax⁡(zS)p=\operatorname{softmax}(z^{S}) and q=softmax⁡(zT)q=\operatorname{softmax}(z^{T}). Because zS=zT−bz^{S}=z^{T}-b, set

δv=−bv+maxu⁡bu.\delta_{v}=-b_{v}+\max_{u}b_{u}.

Assumption 2 gives 0≤δv≤B0\leq\delta_{v}\leq B. Adding a common scalar to logits does not change their softmax, so

pv=qv​eδvZ,Z=∑uqu​eδu≥1.p_{v}=\frac{q_{v}e^{\delta_{v}}}{Z},\qquad Z=\sum_{u}q_{u}e^{\delta_{u}}\geq 1. (12)

First, bound the distance between the two predictive distributions:

TV⁡(p,q)\displaystyle\operatorname{TV}(p,q) =12​Z​∑vqv​|eδv−Z|\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2Z}\sum_{v}q_{v}|e^{\delta_{v}}-Z|
≤12​Z​∑v,uqv​qu​|eδv−eδu|\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{2Z}\sum_{v,u}q_{v}q_{u}|e^{\delta_{v}}-e^{\delta_{u}}|
≤eB−12​(1−∑vqv2).\displaystyle\leq\frac{e^{B}-1}{2}\left(1-\sum_{v}q_{v}^{2}\right). (13)

The first inequality substitutes Z=∑uqu​eδuZ=\sum_{u}q_{u}e^{\delta_{u}} and applies the triangle inequality. The second uses Z≥1Z\geq 1, |eδv−eδu|≤eB−1|e^{\delta_{v}}-e^{\delta_{u}}|\leq e^{B}-1, and the fact that the summand is zero for u=vu=v.

Next, Eq. (12) implies

log⁡pvqv=δv−log⁡Z.\log\frac{p_{v}}{q_{v}}=\delta_{v}-\log Z.

Consequently,

KL(q∥p)\displaystyle\operatorname{KL}(q\|p) =log⁡Z−∑vqv​δv,\displaystyle=\log Z-\sum_{v}q_{v}\delta_{v},
KL(p∥q)\displaystyle\operatorname{KL}(p\|q) =∑vpv​δv−log⁡Z.\displaystyle=\sum_{v}p_{v}\delta_{v}-\log Z. (14)

Adding the two identities cancels the normalization term. With I+={v:pv>qv}I_{+}=\{v:p_{v}>q_{v}\}, the remaining expression obeys

KL(q∥p)+KL(p∥q)\displaystyle\operatorname{KL}(q\|p)+\operatorname{KL}(p\|q)
=∑v(pv−qv)​δv\displaystyle\qquad=\sum_{v}(p_{v}-q_{v})\delta_{v}
≤B​∑v∈I+(pv−qv)=B​TV⁡(p,q).\displaystyle\qquad\leq B\sum_{v\in I_{+}}(p_{v}-q_{v})=B\operatorname{TV}(p,q). (15)

Here the components outside I+I_{+} contribute nonpositive terms, and δv≤B\delta_{v}\leq B on I+I_{+}. Since the reverse KL is nonnegative, combining this inequality with Eq. (13) gives

Fk​(s)≤B⁡(eB−1)2​(1−∑vqv2).F_{k}(s)\leq\frac{B(e^{B}-1)}{2}\left(1-\sum_{v}q_{v}^{2}\right). (16)

Finally, Jensen’s inequality for the convex function −log-\log yields

H⁡(q)=∑vqv​[−log⁡qv]≥−log⁡(∑vqv2).H(q)=\sum_{v}q_{v}[-\log q_{v}]\geq-\log\!\left(\sum_{v}q_{v}^{2}\right).

Thus e−H⁡(q)≤∑vqv2e^{-H(q)}\leq\sum_{v}q_{v}^{2}, and

1−∑vqv2≤1−e−H⁡(q)≤H⁡(q).1-\sum_{v}q_{v}^{2}\leq 1-e^{-H(q)}\leq H(q).

Substituting this relation into Eq. (16), together with the nonnegativity of KL, proves the lemma. ∎

A.3 Proof of Theorem 1

Proof of Theorem 1.

By Assumptions 1 and 2, the common prefix protocol, coverage, and uniform logit contrast condition hold. Lemma 2 therefore establishes the per-prefix loss bound in Eq. (3). In particular, 0≤Fk​(s)≤CB0\leq F_{k}(s)\leq C_{B} on the rollout support and, by coverage, on the current-policy support. Hence both population objectives are finite. Lemma 1 also gives 𝔼μr​[dk,r]≤2\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}[d_{k,r}]\leq 2, ensuring that the product with the bounded loss envelope is integrable.

Apply the change-of-measure lemma and then the entropy-sensitive loss bound pointwise:

Δk\displaystyle\Delta_{k} =|𝔼μr​[(1−ρk,r​(s))​Fk​(s)]|\displaystyle=\left|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}\left[(1-\rho_{k,r}(s))F_{k}(s)\right]\right|
≤𝔼μr​[dk,r​(s)​Fk​(s)]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}\left[d_{k,r}(s)F_{k}(s)\right]
≤CB​𝔼μr​[dk,r​(s)​(1−e−Hk​(s))]\displaystyle\leq C_{B}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}\left[d_{k,r}(s)(1-e^{-H_{k}(s)})\right]
≤CB​𝔼μr​[dk,r​(s)​Hk​(s)].\displaystyle\leq C_{B}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}\left[d_{k,r}(s)H_{k}(s)\right]. (17)

The last step uses 1−e−H≤H1-e^{-H}\leq H for H≥0H\geq 0 and dk,r​(s)≥0d_{k,r}(s)\geq 0. This proves Eq. (4). The product remains inside the expectation throughout, so independence of staleness and entropy is not required. ∎

Sampling probabilities and loss normalization.

The likelihood ratio must describe the actual distributions that generate prefixes. If generation uses a different temperature or other probability transformation, the prefix laws and ratio must use those sampling probabilities; the loss envelope uses the pk,qkp_{k},q_{k} appearing in the KL. Hard top-pp or top-kk truncation can violate coverage and requires separate support handling. The simple product formula also assumes the common fixed token-position distribution in Assumption 1; filtering or response-length normalization may alter the effective training-prefix laws.

Meaning of the two factors.

The staleness signal accumulates probability mismatch over the previous tokens of a prefix. It is not interchangeable with policy update lag or a local one-token rollout KL without an additional argument accounting for earlier positions. Teacher entropy controls the current loss envelope under the contrast assumption; it does not represent a separate cached-target mismatch. Because both learner-side predictions use θk\theta_{k} and the privileged reference is fixed, the comparison changes only the prefix law. The theorem therefore concerns the generating population laws, rather than the empirical distribution of a finite realized buffer.

A.4 Extension to a frozen privileged teacher

We now fix the privileged teacher at the initial parameters θ0\theta_{0}, matching the teacher strategy in Section 5.1. For sh=(x,a,h,y<h)s_{h}=(x,a,h,y_{<h}), define

q0(⋅∣sh)\displaystyle q_{0}(\cdot\mid s_{h}) =πθ0(⋅∣x,a,y<h),\displaystyle=\pi_{\theta_{0}}(\cdot\mid x,a,y_{<h}), (18)
Fkfr​(s)\displaystyle F_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}(s) =KL(q0(⋅∣s)∥pk(⋅∣s)),\displaystyle=\operatorname{KL}\!\left(q_{0}(\cdot\mid s)\,\middle\|\,p_{k}(\cdot\mid s)\right),
H0​(s)\displaystyle H_{0}(s) =−∑v∈𝒱q0(v∣s)logq0(v∣s).\displaystyle=-\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}q_{0}(v\mid s)\log q_{0}(v\mid s).

The teacher and its entropy are fixed functions of the prefix; they can still vary across prefixes. The student and the prefix laws μr,μk\mu_{r},\mu_{k} remain as defined above. Set

Jasync,frk\displaystyle J_{\mathrm{async,fr}}^{k} =𝔼μr​[Fkfr​(s)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}[F_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}(s)], (19)
Jsync,frk\displaystyle J_{\mathrm{sync,fr}}^{k} =𝔼μk​[Fkfr​(s)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{k}}[F_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}(s)],
Δkfr\displaystyle\Delta_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}} =|Jasync,frk−Jsync,frk|.\displaystyle=\left|J_{\mathrm{async,fr}}^{k}-J_{\mathrm{sync,fr}}^{k}\right|.

Both objectives use the same frozen teacher and current student; only their prefix distributions differ.

Assumption 3 (Bounded frozen-teacher logit contrast).

Let q0=softmax⁡(z0T)q_{0}=\operatorname{softmax}(z_{0}^{T}) and pk=softmax⁡(zkS)p_{k}=\operatorname{softmax}(z_{k}^{S}). At the analyzed update, there exists a finite Bkfr≥0B_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}\geq 0 such that, uniformly over the support of μr\mu_{r},

osc⁡(z0T​(s)−zkS​(s))≤Bkfr.\operatorname{osc}\!\left(z_{0}^{T}(s)-z_{k}^{S}(s)\right)\leq B_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}. (20)

The logits are those used in the loss, including any temperature scaling.

Here the contrast is the teacher–student logit difference on the same prefix. Bounding its oscillation is equivalent to bounding the difference in their log odds for every token pair u,vu,v:

|log⁡q0​(v∣s)q0​(u∣s)−log⁡pk​(v∣s)pk​(u∣s)|≤Bkfr.\left|\log\frac{q_{0}(v\mid s)}{q_{0}(u\mid s)}-\log\frac{p_{k}(v\mid s)}{p_{k}(u\mid s)}\right|\leq B_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}.

This is a regularity assumption on the predictive distributions, not an additional training control.

Theorem 2 (Frozen-teacher staleness–entropy bound).

Under Assumptions 1 and 3, let dk,rd_{k,r} be the student prefix staleness in Eq. (9), and write CB=B⁡(eB−1)/2C_{B}=B(e^{B}-1)/2. Then

0≤Fkfr​(s)\displaystyle 0\leq F_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}(s) ≤CBkfr​(1−e−H0​(s))\displaystyle\leq C_{B_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}}(1-e^{-H_{0}(s)}) (21)
≤CBkfr​H0​(s),\displaystyle\leq C_{B_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}}H_{0}(s),

and

Δkfr\displaystyle\Delta_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}} ≤CBkfr​𝔼μr​[dk,r​(s)​(1−e−H0​(s))]\displaystyle\leq C_{B_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}\!\left[d_{k,r}(s)(1-e^{-H_{0}(s)})\right] (22)
≤CBkfr​𝔼μr​[dk,r​(s)​H0​(s)].\displaystyle\leq C_{B_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}\!\left[d_{k,r}(s)H_{0}(s)\right].
Proof.

The proof of Lemma 2 uses only the softmax representations and the bounded oscillation of their logit difference. For a fixed prefix, set b=z0T−zkSb=z_{0}^{T}-z_{k}^{S} and δv=−bv+maxu⁡bu\delta_{v}=-b_{v}+\max_{u}b_{u}. Then 0≤δv≤Bkfr0\leq\delta_{v}\leq B_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}} and

pk​(v∣s)=q0​(v∣s)​eδv∑uq0​(u∣s)​eδu.p_{k}(v\mid s)=\frac{q_{0}(v\mid s)e^{\delta_{v}}}{\sum_{u}q_{0}(u\mid s)e^{\delta_{u}}}.

Thus the same total-variation and symmetric-KL inequalities give

Fkfr​(s)\displaystyle F_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}(s) ≤CBkfr​(1−∑vq0​(v∣s)2)\displaystyle\leq C_{B_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}}\left(1-\sum_{v}q_{0}(v\mid s)^{2}\right)
≤CBkfr​(1−e−H0​(s)).\displaystyle\leq C_{B_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}}(1-e^{-H_{0}(s)}).

Nonnegativity of KL and 1−e−H0≤H01-e^{-H_{0}}\leq H_{0} prove Eq. (21). In particular, the loss is bounded on both prefix supports. By the same change of measure as in Lemma 1,

Δkfr\displaystyle\Delta_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}} =|𝔼μr​[(1−ρk,r​(s))​Fkfr​(s)]|\displaystyle=\left|\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}\left[(1-\rho_{k,r}(s))F_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}(s)\right]\right|
≤𝔼μr​[dk,r​(s)​Fkfr​(s)].\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{r}}\!\left[d_{k,r}(s)F_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}(s)\right].

Substitution gives Eq. (22). ∎

Accounting for student drift.

The frozen-teacher contrast assumption must be checked separately from Assumption 2. An optional sufficient condition separates the initial teacher–student difference from subsequent student drift. Let z0Sz_{0}^{S} denote the initial student’s logits. If, uniformly over the analyzed rollout support,

osc⁡(z0T​(s)−z0S​(s))\displaystyle\operatorname{osc}(z_{0}^{T}(s)-z_{0}^{S}(s)) ≤Binit,\displaystyle\leq B_{\mathrm{init}}, (23)
osc⁡(zkS​(s)−z0S​(s))\displaystyle\operatorname{osc}(z_{k}^{S}(s)-z_{0}^{S}(s)) ≤Dk,\displaystyle\leq D_{k},

then subadditivity of oscillation yields

osc⁡(z0T−zkS)\displaystyle\operatorname{osc}(z_{0}^{T}-z_{k}^{S}) ≤osc⁡(z0T−z0S)\displaystyle\leq\operatorname{osc}(z_{0}^{T}-z_{0}^{S})
+osc⁡(zkS−z0S)\displaystyle\quad+\operatorname{osc}(z_{k}^{S}-z_{0}^{S})
≤Binit+Dk.\displaystyle\leq B_{\mathrm{init}}+D_{k}.

Hence Binit+DkB_{\mathrm{init}}+D_{k} is one admissible choice of BkfrB_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}; the theorem only requires Assumption 3, not this decomposition. Freezing the teacher does not itself bound accumulated student drift or guarantee the same numerical constant as in the evolving-teacher case. A bound on rollout age k−rk-r also does not by itself bound drift from initialization.

Implications and scope.

The same interaction between prefix staleness and teacher entropy therefore holds for a frozen teacher under the stated contrast bound. In particular, μr=μk\mu_{r}=\mu_{k} implies Δkfr=0\Delta_{k}^{\mathrm{fr}}=0, even if the current student differs substantially from the teacher. There is no teacher-version mismatch on a fixed prefix: cached and recomputed frozen-teacher predictions coincide when the privileged context and evaluation settings are unchanged. Low teacher entropy alone cannot ensure a small distillation loss without a uniform bound on the teacher–student logit contrast: for qϵ=(1−ϵ,ϵ)q_{\epsilon}=(1-\epsilon,\epsilon) and p=(1/2,1/2)p=(1/2,1/2), H⁡(qϵ)→0H(q_{\epsilon})\to 0 but KL(qϵ∥p)→log2\operatorname{KL}(q_{\epsilon}\|p)\to\log 2 as ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0; the logit contrast then diverges.

Appendix B Experiment Details

B.1 Staleness-Cutoff Ablation

We evaluate maximum rollout age K∈{4,6,8,10}K\in\{4,6,8,10\} on Qwen3-1.7B using eight A100s split into four learner and four actor GPUs, with policy export interval sync_step=2\texttt{sync\_step}=2, clipping threshold c=0.05c=0.05, and uniform token weights (βH=0\beta_{H}=0). This configuration is the staleness-control-only variant; vanilla AsyncOPSD has no active age cutoff.

Table 7 reports the directly measured results of this additional sweep. We compute relative throughput as RK=v¯K/v¯6R_{K}=\bar{v}_{K}/\bar{v}_{6}, where v¯K\bar{v}_{K} is the mean accepted-sample throughput across the three executions at KK. The denominator is the measured K=6K=6 mean from this sweep; the absolute measurements in Table 3 come from separate executions and are retained. The rejection percentage covers claimed microbatches and excludes generated samples left in the queue at shutdown.

Tightening the cutoff to K=4K=4 lowers mean accepted staleness to 3.79 and rejects about one third of claimed rollouts. At K=6K=6, mean throughput increases to 9.22 samples/s and rejection drops to 10.70%. Relaxing the cutoff to K=8K=8 yields a further 11.4% throughput gain, accompanied by older accepted rollouts. No rejections occur at K=8K=8 or K=10K=10 in these executions, and their mean throughputs are similar. We retain K=6K=6 to enforce a tighter age bound while preserving most of the observed peak throughput.

B.2 Entropy-Weighting Ablation

We evaluate the entropy-weighting coefficient βH\beta_{H} on Qwen3-1.7B using AIME 2025. Table 8 reports Avg@12 for four coefficients. The selected value βH=0.1\beta_{H}=0.1 achieves the highest score, 43.90, while both the smaller coefficient 0.03 and the larger coefficients 0.3 and 1.0 yield lower scores. These results support βH=0.1\beta_{H}=0.1 within the tested model and benchmark.
